M-VAVE FM-1 firmware for inhospitable soundscapes

Norilsk is not made for musical niceties. There are no pretty chords here, no polite arpeggios, no presets that flatter. It is made for ambient hellscapes and barren, grim atmospheres: drones that never resolve, textures that corrode as they hold, noise that does not apologise. Sound for places nobody should have to live in.

It is named after Norilsk, the nickel-smelting city above the Arctic Circle: built by prisoners of the Gulag, closed to outsiders, sunk in polar night for weeks each winter, its air thick with sulphur dioxide, its rivers turned red by the works upstream. Every sound here is drawn at random, wired at random into effects drawn at random, and torn apart at will: as fit for noise experiments as for slow, dark ambient.

How the machine is put together

Three generators make sound; three effect slots wreck it; a master delay and plate reverb close the chain. The white keys play the generator chosen last, in the scale chosen; four voices are shared between the three. Each generator is wired by cables into one, two or three effects anywhere in the effect slots, and keeps a dry share of its own. Each effect slot is a chain of two or three effects; any of them may also be wired across into a later slot, or out to the master on its own. The first processor core renders the voices, the second runs the effects, a block behind.

Every generator is a MOLECULE: six-operator FM whose operators read band-limited waves as well as sines, bent by phase distortion, written into a buffer of half a second and read back as grains, as a cloud or a stream of pulsars. An invisible hand keeps moving each voice's macros, so a held note never holds still; Russolo's grit drops its bits, crosses it with itself and makes it stutter. Every sound swells in and keeps moving, and nothing sounds on once no note is held, latched or looped: released voices fade out within three seconds, and the effect slots close two seconds after the last, while the master delay's and reverb's tails ring out whole.

Randomness, level by level

Almost nothing in Norilsk is set by hand at the start: it is drawn. What you do is choose, keep, throw again, and play. The draws are made at every scale, from the inside of a single note to the whole machine:

  1. The sound. MOLECULE draws a sound from a family, a seed, a path and an engine generation, bit for bit the same every time it is asked: a sound is kept as its seed, and a session brings it back exactly. Twenty families: METAL, DRONE, BRUIT, GLASS, CLOUD, SHATTER, FREEZE, FURNACE, HUM, STATIC, HOWL, SCRAPE, DATA, ASH, TUNNEL and more.
  2. The note in motion. Inside every voice the invisible hand drifts the brightness, detune, grain and motion; the grit stage cuts bits and stutters from points of its own; the grains are taken from places that wander. The same key held twice never sounds the same twice.
  3. The generator (HOME on a generator): a scene, a family weighed by how harsh it may be, how many effects it is cabled into and where, its dry share. (One generator modulates another only when you link them by hand.)
  4. The effect slot (HOME on an effect slot): one of 22 recipes, each place filled from the recipe's choices that fit the slot's memory, every value drawn around its home, the outs, the cables across to the slots after it.
  5. The paths. ABRASIVE (gnarly, textural, torn) and DARK (drones, depression, a little quieter) lean every draw above: the scenes, the families, the recipes, the effects' values. Neither on: anything goes.
  6. Partial throws. REWIRE draws only the cables; RAND PARAMS only an effect slot's values, or a generator's sound within its family; SHIFT + HOME keeps the family or the recipe; HOME held throws all six slots at once.
  7. Modulation. SHIFT + SEQ throws a slot's two LFOs (shape, rate, mode, fade) and two to six of its eight routes; the STEPS and DRIFT shapes and the RANDOM source keep drawing as it plays.
  8. Playing. The DISINTEGRATOR gates, stutters, crushes and throws each generator about the stereo image in pulses of random length; the looper's VARY redraws every note it plays, and RANDOM jumps through the loops.
  9. What chance does not touch. A snapshot is the whole machine, every value and every cable, the latched notes and the loops' playing: sixteen to a session, sixty-four sessions, recalled exactly or morphed into over up to thirty seconds.

Features

Three generators
Each a MOLECULE voice with its level, pan, sends, mute, looper and DISINTEGRATOR.
Nineteen effects
FILTER, FOLD, MULAW, SHIFT, MODAL, STRING, VOWEL, DELAY, TAPE, REVERSE, SPRING, REVERB, GLITCH, CLOUD, SCREAM, RING, STARVE, CHEB, BANK — drawn into three slots by 22 recipes, with cables between slots.
DISINTEGRATOR
KNOB 1: an unstable gate on each generator — stutters, crushes, sudden throws across the image — more erratic the higher.
Draw paths
ABRASIVE and DARK, on two black keys, lean everything HOME draws.
Snapshots
Sixteen whole-machine states to a session, morphed into over 0 to 30 seconds.
Sessions
Sixty-four, saved in the FM-1's flash, and backed up to a computer from this site.
Modulation
Two LFOs and eight routes on every slot, onto macros, levels, pans, sends and any effect's values.
Loopers
Tonitor's looper on each generator: ten loops, overdubs, reverse, pendulum, random, half and double speed.
Master
Tonitor's delay and plate reverb, a send per generator; their tails always ring out.
USB audio
The FM-1 is a class-compliant audio interface: record the master straight into a computer.
A readable screen
Few words, very large, high contrast: made for low vision.

Norilsk runs on the M-VAVE FM-1 (JieLi AC791N). It is unofficial: see the install page before installing.

Developed by Nuno Zimas. Firmware: GPL-3.0. Website and logo: MIT. Source on GitHub.

M-VAVE and FM-1 are trademarks of their owner, used only to say which device Norilsk runs on. Norilsk is named after the city; it has nothing to do with the company that runs its smelters.
